name: Tesa/IPA Protocol

lead: Tesa/IPA stacks two growth-hormone-axis peptides, tesamorelin and ipamorelin, and is used for fat loss, especially around the midsection, and a leaner look.

Tesamorelin mimics growth-hormone-releasing hormone and ipamorelin acts on the ghrelin receptor, so both raise growth hormone and IGF-1 through different routes. Tesamorelin is a prescription drug approved for HIV-associated lipodystrophy, where trials looked at visceral fat. Ipamorelin was developed for postoperative ileus and dropped. No trial has tested the combination.

paras: In peptide circles the stack is run alongside diet and training for body composition, with fat-loss changes described over weeks to months. Tesamorelin is prescription-only and ipamorelin is typically sold as a research peptide.

Tesamorelin effects reported in its use include injection-site reactions, edema, joint pain and glucose intolerance. Ipamorelin is unapproved and on the WADA prohibited list. The combination has no safety data.

angle.text: Tesa/IPA aims at a leaner midsection: both peptides raise growth hormone, which is linked to less visceral fat. Tesamorelin has trial data for visceral fat in a specific patient group; the combination has not been trialled.

lead: The Tesa/IPA protocol is a name used in peptide and body-composition circles for pairing two injectable growth-hormone-axis peptides, tesamorelin and ipamorelin, with the aim of a leaner, more defined physique. The two are different substances: tesamorelin is a synthetic analogue of growth-hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH), while ipamorelin is a pentapeptide that acts on the ghrelin (growth hormone secretagogue) receptor.[1][2][3]

The looks chain people describe is: more growth hormone release, raising IGF-1, lowering body fat (particularly around the abdomen) and supporting lean mass, which gives a sharper waist and more visible muscle. Tesamorelin's recognised effect in its approved use is lipolysis, the breakdown of fat, and trials in HIV-associated abdominal fat accumulation report reductions in visceral fat, waist circumference and trunk fat alongside gains in lean mass.[1][4]

Tesamorelin is a prescription drug developed by Theratechnologies and sold as Egrifta, first approved in 2010 for HIV-associated lipodystrophy.[1] Ipamorelin was developed by Novo Nordisk, later tested by Helsinn Therapeutics for postoperative ileus, where development stopped because of lack of efficacy; it is not an approved drug and is commonly sold as a research peptide.[2]

Proponents pair the two because they release growth hormone through different receptors. No published trial has tested the combination in humans.[1][2] On T Nation, one user reported that IGF-1 rose above 300 on tesamorelin plus ipamorelin but barely moved on a CJC/ipamorelin pairing, and described the former as the option they would return to.[5]

paras: Tesamorelin consists of the full 44 amino acids of human GHRH with a trans-3-hexenoic acid group added, which makes it more potent and more resistant to breakdown than natural GHRH. It stimulates the body's own growth hormone release, raising IGF-1, and its main effect on body fat is lipolysis. [1]

Reported adverse effects include injection-site redness and itching, peripheral edema, diarrhea and joint or limb pain; it may cause glucose intolerance and raise type 2 diabetes risk, and it is contraindicated in pregnancy and in patients with hypothalamic-pituitary disruption. [1]

Pharmacokinetically, Wikipedia lists tesamorelin's bioavailability as 4 percent or less after injection and its elimination half-life as roughly 26 to 38 minutes, with clearance by proteolysis and renal routes [1]. The molecule has the formula C221H366N72O67S and a molar mass of about 5,136 g/mol [1]. Its brand names are Egrifta, Egrifta SV and Egrifta WR [1]. The one clinical study the Wikipedia article cites is a randomised, placebo-controlled trial with a safety extension in HIV-infected patients with abdominal fat accumulation, published by Falutz and colleagues in 2010 [1].

Ipamorelin is a synthetic pentapeptide derived from GHRP-1 that selectively agonises the ghrelin receptor. It raises plasma growth hormone in animals and humans and, unlike GHRP-2 and GHRP-6, is reported not to stimulate ACTH or cortisol. Its elimination half-life is about two hours. [2]
Helsinn's phase II program for postoperative ileus stopped because of lack of efficacy. It appears among WADA-prohibited substances and has been used by athletes as a performance-enhancing drug. [2]

Chemically, ipamorelin has the sequence Aib-His-D-2-Nal-D-Phe-Lys-NH2 (formula C38H49N9O5, molar mass about 712 g/mol) [2]. It does not appear to affect prolactin, FSH, LH or TSH, and the article describes it as highly selective for growth hormone secretion; it can be given intravenously or subcutaneously in research settings [2]. Novo Nordisk's development code for it was NNC 26-0161 [2].

Growth hormone secretagogues fall into two receptor families. Ghrelin-receptor agonists, which include ipamorelin, GHRP-6, GHRP-2 and the oral compound MK-677, mimic the hunger hormone ghrelin; GHRH-receptor agonists, which include sermorelin, CJC-1295 and tesamorelin, mimic growth-hormone-releasing hormone.[3] The Tesa/IPA idea combines one agent from each family, so the pituitary receives a release signal through two separate routes.[3]

Wikipedia's account of tesamorelin says it stimulates the body's own growth hormone release, raising IGF-1, and attributes its fat reduction mainly to lipolysis followed by lower triglycerides.[1] Ipamorelin is reported to raise plasma growth hormone in animals and humans without stimulating ACTH or cortisol, and not to affect prolactin, FSH, LH or TSH, whereas many secretagogues also raise cortisol or prolactin.[2][3]

The one trial cited by Wikipedia's tesamorelin article is a randomised, placebo-controlled study with a safety extension in HIV-infected patients with abdominal fat accumulation, published by Falutz and colleagues in 2010.[1] A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis pooled four randomised trials with 909 patients and reported reductions in visceral adipose tissue, waist circumference and trunk fat and increases in lean body mass at the labelled dose, with modest improvement in total cholesterol; it noted growth-hormone-related adverse effects, higher discontinuation with tesamorelin (relative risk 2.25, 95% CI 0.98 to 5.17) and limited long-term safety data.[4]

Secondary analyses of two phase III trials define a responder as someone with at least an 8 percent fall in visceral fat, about 70 percent of treated participants in one analysis; responders showed improvements in fat density and in muscle area and density, and those with raised liver enzymes had greater drops in liver enzymes than non-responders.[4] These participants had HIV and abdominal obesity and were mostly men.[4]

Ipamorelin's published human work is small: a healthy-volunteer pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic model, and a postoperative ileus programme that Helsinn discontinued for lack of efficacy.[2] Rat studies describe longitudinal bone growth and increased bone mineral content, which are the studies looksmax.org users cite in height discussions.[2][6]

Recent reviews say human evidence for many self-administered peptides is thin. A 2026 scoping review in the American Journal of Sports Medicine of six peptides including ipamorelin found about 67 percent of identified publications used animal models, and a 2026 review in Sexual Medicine Reviews found growth hormone secretagogues reliably raise growth hormone and IGF-1, with limited evidence for improved sexual function or physical performance.[4]

Reported adverse effects of tesamorelin include injection-site redness and itching, peripheral edema, diarrhea and joint or limb pain; it may cause glucose intolerance and raise type 2 diabetes risk, and it is contraindicated in pregnancy and in patients with hypothalamic-pituitary disruption.[1]

The FDA lists ipamorelin acetate under Category 2 of its interim policy for bulk drug substances used in compounding, added 29 September 2023, citing possible immunogenicity from aggregation or peptide-related impurities, difficulty characterising a peptide with unnatural amino acids, and a study linking intravenous use for gastric motility to serious adverse events including death.[7] For CJC-1295, the FDA page says the nomination was withdrawn and that the agency has identified serious adverse events including increased heart rate and a systemic vasodilatory reaction, with limited clinical data.[7]

A 2026 Missouri Medicine review describes risks of unregulated injectable peptides generally, including contamination, inaccurate dosing, cardiovascular stress and carcinogenesis concerns, and notes these products lack established human safety data.[4]

Tesamorelin was developed by the Canadian company Theratechnologies and was first approved in the United States in 2010 as Egrifta for HIV-associated lipodystrophy, the abnormal accumulation of abdominal fat in people on antiretroviral therapy.[1] Later formulations carry the names Egrifta SV and Egrifta WR.[1]

Ipamorelin was introduced in the late 1990s as a selective growth hormone secretagogue. Wikipedia credits a 1998 paper by Raun and colleagues in the European Journal of Endocrinology with describing it as the first selective compound of its type, followed by 1999 work reporting longitudinal bone growth in rats and a pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic model in healthy volunteers.[2] Helsinn Therapeutics later took it into phase II testing for postoperative ileus after bowel resection; a 2014 proof-of-concept randomised study was published and the programme was discontinued for lack of efficacy.[2]

The GHRH-side partner most often paired with ipamorelin in forums is CJC-1295, developed by ConjuChem Biotechnologies and tested in phase II for lipodystrophy and growth hormone deficiency; Wikipedia reports that its development stopped in 2006 after a trial subject died, which the attending physician believed was likely due to undiagnosed coronary artery disease unrelated to the drug.[8] The pairing of tesamorelin with ipamorelin as a named combination appears to be a product of peptide-vendor and body-composition forum culture rather than of any clinical programme; looksmax.org threads more often discuss ipamorelin with CJC-1295 than with tesamorelin.[9][10]

Proponents describe the two peptides as complementary: a GHRH analogue amplifies the pituitary's growth-hormone pulses, while a ghrelin-receptor agonist triggers a release through a second pathway. Ipamorelin is reported to raise growth hormone without stimulating ACTH or cortisol, which proponents cite as a reason it is chosen over other secretagogues.[2]

Forum users commonly track IGF-1 blood tests as their marker of response. In a T Nation thread on growth hormone, one poster compared tesamorelin/ipamorelin with CJC/ipamorelin by IGF-1 values and noted tesamorelin-based stacks cost more than CJC-based ones while remaining cheaper than pharmaceutical growth hormone.[5] A separate T Nation member described liking CJC-1295 and ipamorelin alongside lipid and diet changes, and another thread links tesamorelin to a clinician's talk on pregnenolone and aromatase inhibitors.[11][12]

On looksmax.org, ipamorelin is more often discussed in combination with CJC-1295 for height, muscle or general growth in younger users, and a thread asks whether tesamorelin interacts with a CJC-1295/ipamorelin regimen.[9][10]

Both substances appear on the World Anti-Doping Agency's prohibited list, and Wikipedia notes athlete use of ipamorelin as a performance-enhancing drug, citing media coverage of peptides in Major League Baseball in 2016 and NBA suspensions in 2018 and 2019 (the cited reports do not all name ipamorelin specifically).[1][2] Tesamorelin is prescription-only in the United States, while ipamorelin has no approved legal status and is sold by vendors as a research peptide.[1][2]

In looksmax.org threads, younger users with open growth plates ask whether growth-hormone secretagogues could add height or facial bone growth, and cite the rat bone-growth work.[6] In one long post, a former short, overweight teenager wrote that he had bought ipamorelin and CJC-1295 but, after the purchase, saw an endocrinologist instead and was glad he had not used them.[6] Other replies in the same thread described ipamorelin as similar to the oral secretagogue MK-677 and pointed to a rat study of bone mineral content.[6]

Clinicians have started writing about online self-administration of performance-enhancing peptides: a 2026 Frontiers in Endocrinology review proposes a clinical algorithm for taking exposure histories and communicating risk.[4]

Related compounds discussed alongside the pairing include CJC-1295 with or without DAC, sermorelin, GHRP-2, GHRP-6, MK-677 and pharmaceutical growth hormone; Wikipedia groups secretagogues by whether they act on the ghrelin or the GHRH receptor.[3] T Nation members compare the cost of peptide stacks with pharmaceutical growth hormone.[5]

No published human study has tested tesamorelin and ipamorelin together, for fat loss or any cosmetic purpose. Tesamorelin has been studied in randomised trials in HIV-associated abdominal fat accumulation, and ipamorelin in a postoperative ileus trial and a healthy-volunteer pharmacokinetic study.[1][2][4] Ipamorelin has also been examined in rat studies of bone growth, which looksmax.org users cite in height discussions; these are animal research.[6]

lore.intro: The combination is discussed in peptide-oriented body-composition circles as a fat-loss and growth-hormone stack, and ipamorelin more broadly appears in looksmax.org height and body-composition threads.[5][6][9]
